newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Berlin grapples with money woes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Berlin grapples with money woes.

text.p: The lights have gone off in Berlin's Schoeneberg city hall and there is no hot water in the building where U.S. president John F. Kennedy paid his historic tribute to the city's lonely Cold War ordeal.

Under enormous pressure to save money, the city once split by the Iron Curtain can no longer afford the electricity to keep the lifts operating in the building where Kennedy delivered his famous "Ich bin ein Berliner" speech in 1963.
Seven years after the Berlin Wall was brought down, freedom's most famous outpost is broke.

More than 50 billion marks ($33.06 billion) in debt, Berlin has been forced to make draconian spending cuts that are -- quite literally -- leaving people in the dark. The debt level has more than tripled since the Wall was breached on November 9, 1989.

"We have to save money everywhere we can think of," said Otto Edel, a Schoeneberg councillor. The district has even begun renting out the stately building where Kennedy said he was "proud to be a Berliner" for private parties and dances.
In the building's hallways and other non-essential rooms, lights have been switched off. "It can get pretty dark in here after the sun sets," Edel said.
Even with the spending cuts, the debt will hit 76 billion marks by the time the government moves from Bonn to Berlin in 1999. That is 22,000 marks for every Berliner.

"We are caught in a very difficult transition," said Annette Fugmann-Heesing, the city-state's new finance minister and an outspoken critic of Berlin's failure to wean itself sooner from lavish federal subisides that vanished with the Wall.
The loathed cuts are also exacerbating tensions between the formerly communist east and west Berlin, once a free market enclave surrounded by the 155 km (96-mile) long Berlin Wall.
The economic and social upheaval has certainly left deep scars in east Berlin, where it is hard not to overhear disparaging remarks about "arrogant" and "selfish" westerners.

But the cuts in expenditure have struck particularly raw nerves in west Berlin, where the eroded standard of living is blamed on the fall of the Wall. It usually doesn't take west Berliners long to remind those who will listen of the financial sacrifices they have made since the Wall fell.

Because of its isolated position in the middle of communist East Germany, West Berlin grew accustomed to pampered treatment from the Bonn government. It received special subsidies that were used as an inducement to stop people from leaving.
The lavish subsidies were introduced after the Wall was built in 1961 and quickly eliminated after it fell. But very, very fond memories of that extra cash linger on.
An eight percent "Berlin Bonus" on pay cheques given to workers by the government was among the most cherished federal subsidies during the Cold War. That is long gone.

At the same time pay was shrinking, west Berliners were confronted with a frightening surge in the cost of living and a deteriorating quality of life. Housing prices doubled. Unemployment hit 15 percent. The crime rate multiplied.

"The people in the west have less money in their pockets than before," said Edel, a councillor in the western district of Schoeneberg. "That is something they feel constantly and it contributes to a sense of dissatisfaction."
With Berlin's finances in a shambles, the latest round of cuts in local services makes the longing for the more financially comfortable days of the Cold War more acute.

Entrance fees for swimming pools were recently doubled to eight marks, rubbish collection fees raised by 30 percent, an annual "dog tax" nearly doubled to 300 marks and escalators to many underground rail stations have been turned off because there is no money in the budget for repairs.

Plans to build a museum about the Gestapo were cancelled because there was no money. And 3,000 schoolchildren packed a cathedral to pray for their school after the authorities said it would be closed because of budget constraints.

"The frustration especially in west Berlin is understandable," said Karin Noelte, city editor for the Neues Deutschland daily that was the official Communist Party organ in East Berlin and survived with a loyal eastern readership.
"The west Berliners have lost a lot of money and there are plenty of opportunistic politicians out there trying to capitalise on that frustration," she added.

Despite the financial squeeze, many westerners have remained loyal to the ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) who pander to their faithful constituents. The CDU is by far the strongest party in west Berlin but extremely weak in the east.

During testy negotiations between the CDU and their coalition partners the Social Democrats, it was clear that efforts to try to close a seven billion mark deficit in the 46 billion mark budget for 1997 were hampered by the CDU's resistance to further cuts that would upset western voters.

Berlin CDU leader Klaus Landowsky said the city had to watch out "lest Berlin be brought down to a level of mouse-gray bleakness found everywhere in east Germany". It was a remark that didn't exactly promote a spirit of German unity.
"Landowsky is dividing Berlin with comments like that," said Martin Federlein, the head of the CDU in east Berlin. "A lot of easterners felt their honour attacked by him."
Dieter Vesper, an economist at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW) in Berlin said there was a danger the latest cuts will deepen the gulf between the east and west.
He said the city's problems were magnified after the Wall was brought down because there was two of everything: city administrations, police forces, school systems and fire departments.

"There was a bloated city bureacracy in the west and east even before the Wall fell and they couldn't just lay everyone off," Vesper said. "It has taken time to integrate and it is a very expensive process. At the same time, the federal government pulled out of the financing for Berlin."

Adding to those woes, the industrial base in both east and west Berlin has been badly eroded in recent years -- hundreds of companies have either folded or moved to sites outside the city where the land and labour are far cheaper.
"The economic developments have lagged far beneath our expectations," said Frank Zimmermann, spokesman for the city's finance ministry. "We could have seen this coming."
But maybe it was already too dark in city hall. ($1=1.5125 Mark)
